concept.name: Multiple testing problem
concept.definition: The inflation of false-positive rates when many hypotheses are tested simultaneously: at a per-test level alpha, the probability of at least one false rejection across m tests grows toward 1 as m increases, so unadjusted testing reliably produces spurious discoveries.
concept.intuition: A 5% test cries wolf one time in twenty by design; test a hundred strategies and you should expect about five wolves even if every strategy is worthless.
concept.mechanics: The familywise error rate (probability of any false rejection) is controlled by Bonferroni (alpha/m) or Holm's step-down procedure; the false discovery rate is controlled by the Benjamini-Hochberg step-up procedure. In finance, Harvey, Liu and Zhu (2016) argue that the factor literature requires t-statistic thresholds well above 2 for exactly this reason.
concept.formula: FWER = P(at least one false rejection); Bonferroni rejects H_i when p_i <= alpha/m, giving FWER <= alpha.
concept.failure_modes: FWER control is conservative with many or correlated tests and destroys power, while FDR control assumes independence or positive dependence and needs the Benjamini-Yekutieli correction under arbitrary dependence.
concept.misconceptions: That a single strong p-value is immune to multiplicity: what matters is how many hypotheses were examined to produce it, and p = 0.01 found among 200 tests is unremarkable under the null.
concept.example: Scanning 300 calendar anomalies at alpha = 0.05 yields about 15 significant effects under pure chance; Bonferroni demands p < 0.00017 before declaring any of them real.
